title: Safe vs Unsafe Rotation
shortDefinition: Safe rotation occurs when knee line is free and heel is hidden; unsafe rotation occurs when knee line is trapped and heel is exposed.
whyItMatters: Leg lock injuries usually come from turning the wrong direction in an entanglement — knowing when to turn and when to stop is technical safety.
deepExplanation: Safety assessment in order: (1) Is the heel exposed? (2) Is the knee line trapped? (3) Is the secondary leg controlled? If all 3 signals are present, do not rotate — tap or free yourself first. If heel hidden and knee free, you can rotate safely.
beginnerView: Do not rotate hard when the heel is exposed and the knee is trapped.
advancedView: Use rotation sensing to bait: let them feel knee line is trapped then change direction.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Safe vs Unsafe Rotation during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Safe vs Unsafe Rotation to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Safe vs Unsafe Rotation is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Safe vs Unsafe Rotation before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
